There is a symmetric OutboundPolicyServer, L29 for routing decisions the proxy makes on the way out. The glue between index and servers is thin: InboundDiscover, L23 implements the discover trait with get_inbound_server, L39, cloning the current snapshot out of the shared index. Reading this stack bottom-up, you can trace a ServerAuthorization YAML file all the way from a Kubernetes watch to a protobuf Authz message inside a hundred lines of code.

Destination: Addresses on the Wire, Profiles on the Rails

The destination service is the proxy’s phone book, and it is the Go heart of the control plane. Main, L28 boots it on port 8086 with a wall of flags for trust domain, cluster domain, and opaque ports. The server built by NewServer, L87 implements two streaming APIs. Get, L148 answers “where can I reach this destination” by subscribing to endpoint updates, and GetProfile, L313 answers “how should I treat requests to it” by streaming service profiles that carry per-route retry and timeout configuration.

The address side is worth a look because it is where Kubernetes vocabulary turns into mesh vocabulary. NewEndpointsWatcher, L83 watches Endpoints and EndpointSlices and publishes address sets per service. Downstream, endpointTranslator, L35 converts those sets into the Destination.Get protobuf stream the proxy consumes, and newEndpointTranslator, L76 captures per-pod details like topology zone so the proxy can prefer same-zone endpoints. For an inference stack, this is the machinery that lets you scale the decode workers behind one Service and have every meshed client re-resolve without restarting anything.

Identity: mTLS Without Ceremony

Every meshed workload gets a certificate naming it in a trust domain, and the issuance path is compact. The identity controller starts from Main, L32 and serves the Certify gRPC API implemented by Certify, L212. That method’s first job is validation: the K8sTokenValidator, L26 turns the workload’s service-account bearer token into a Kubernetes TokenReview, and its Validate, L51 method maps the authenticated username — the system:serviceaccount:namespace:name form — into a Linkerd identity. Only then does the service sign a certificate bound to that identity.

The client side is charmingly explicit: the proxy-identity init container runs before the proxy starts and blocks until it holds a cert. In practice this is why Linkerd’s “zero-config mTLS” claim holds up: nothing in your deployment YAML changes, because the injector already added the init container and the volume mounts that make the handshake possible.

From Install to Your First Model

Enough reading; here is the shortest path from nothing to a meshed inference service, with each step tied to the code that implements it.

First, install the control plane. The CLI entry point newCmdInstall, L89 loads the linkerd-control-plane and linkerd-crds charts (install.go, L38) and renders them with the embedded Helm engine, so the canonical invocation is simply:

linkerd install --crds | kubectl apply -f -
linkerd install    | kubectl apply -f -
linkerd check

newCmdCheck, L92 runs the health checks that verify control-plane pods, webhooks, and API availability before you proceed.

Second, mesh the workloads. You have two ways to add the sidecar. Client-side, NewCmdInject, L50 pipes a manifest through runInjectCmd, L46, and the patch is built by the same ResourceConfig, L629 machinery the webhook uses. Automatic sidecar injection goes through the admission webhook whose Inject, L31 handler is invoked by the Kubernetes API server on pod creation. For a model server, annotate the namespace once and deploy:

kubectl create ns infer && kubectl annotate ns infer linkerd.io/inject=enabled
kubectl apply -f vllm-deploy.yaml -n infer

Third, lock the door. By default, Linkerd’s policy is deny-with-allow-lists once you define a Server for the port. Create a Server selecting your vLLM port, then a ServerAuthorization permitting only your gateway’s identity. The Rust index (saz updates, L25) picks the change up, watch_port streams the new authorizations to the sidecar, and within a watch tick only meshed, authenticated clients get through. The policy kinds are real Kubernetes CRDs in the policy.linkerd.io group, as the protobuf labels (inbound.rs, L238) confirm. A similar gate in front of a metrics sidecar is exactly how you would expose a Prometheus scrape port to the mesh safely.

Honest Limits

A few things this repo tour cannot give you. Most importantly: the data-plane proxy is not here. The README’s repo list is explicit that linkerd2-proxy, L26 — “Linkerd 2.x data plane proxy” — and the gRPC API bindings at linkerd2-proxy-api are separate repositories. What this repo contains is everything around the proxy: the policy decisions it enforces, the addresses it discovers, the certificates it holds, and the containers that install it. If you want to read the Rust HTTP/2 implementation or the byte-level latency tricks, you must go one repository further.

Second, scope: this tour covers the four directories that dominate the control-plane story (cli/, controller/, pkg/, policy-controller/), not the viz/metrics extensions, the multicluster link controller, or the Helm charts in full. Third, no performance numbers here: Linkerd’s latency claims live in its official documentation and benchmarks, and I have not reproduced them — the only thing I claim from source is what each symbol does. Finally, all line numbers point at main as of 2026-11-02; Rust workspaces reorganize often, so treat the links as a snapshot and grep if a symbol has moved. What survives the drift is the architecture: a small Go control plane, a strict Rust policy brain, and a proxy that needs surprisingly little from both to make a model-serving cluster secure by default.
entry.summary: A source tour of Linkerd's Go control plane, Rust policy controller, and the seams that keep it the lightest mesh for Kubernetes.

entry.title: Traefik in the Source: How a Go Reverse Proxy Learns Your Fleet and Rewires Itself Live

link.title: Traefik in the Source: How a Go Reverse Proxy Learns Your Fleet and Rewires Itself Live

entry.content:
If you run more than one model server — a vLLM box here, a FastAPI inference container there, a GPU node pool over in Kubernetes — then the most performance-critical piece of software you own is not the model server. It is the thing that decides, in microseconds, which of those servers should receive the next request. That decision is made at the edge, by a reverse proxy, and when the edge is wrong everything behind it looks slow. Token streams stall while requests sit in the wrong queue. Canaries never get tested under real load. Rolling out a new model version becomes a maintenance window instead of a config edit.

Traefik approaches this problem from an unusual angle. Instead of asking you to describe every route up front, it watches your infrastructure — Docker engines, Kubernetes APIs, plain files — and builds the routing table itself, then keeps rebuilding it as your fleet changes. Need to route api.example.com/v1/embeddings to an embedding fleet and /v1/chat to a chat fleet? With the right provider wired in, you declare that intent where your services already live (labels, CRDs, files) and Traefik translates it into live listeners with zero restarts. For AI/ML workloads this matters more than it sounds: inference fleets scale horizontally, GPU nodes come and go, and you want the routing layer to track reality automatically while you still control weights for canary rollouts of a new checkpoint.

This post is a source-level tour of how Traefik actually does that, read directly from the Go code on the master branch. The two diagrams below were generated from the repository structure: first an overview of the major subsystems, then a deeper pass over the same architecture with the bootstrap, config and routing internals included. Every symbol linked in the text points at a real function in the repository, so you can follow along line by line.

Traefik's main subsystems: the bootstrap wires providers, a configuration watcher, entrypoints and router factories; requests flow from entrypoints through the muxer into load-balanced services; the API exposes runtime state for the dashboard.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Bootstrap. main, L54 parses static configuration and calls setupServer, L180, the single function that assembles every manager, factory and entrypoint you see in the diagram.
  • Providers. NewProviderAggregator, L181 builds the aggregator whose Provide, L178 launches all configured providers against one shared channel — Docker, Kubernetes, files and friends all pushing configuration messages into the same stream.
  • The watcher. NewConfigurationWatcher, L324 creates the core hot-reload loop: receiveConfigurations, L98 deduplicates provider updates and applyConfigurations, L166 merges and broadcasts them.
  • Entrypoints. NewTCPEntryPoint, L184 builds each listener — a keep-alive TCP socket from buildListener, L512 plus one or two Go HTTP servers from newHTTPServer, L643.
  • Routers. CreateRouters, L101 builds HTTP, TCP and UDP routers per entrypoint; the HTTP side goes through NewManager, L55 which validates the router tree in ParseRouterTree, L91.
  • Rules. NewParser, L31 is a predicate parser that turns strings like Host(api.example.com) && PathPrefix(/v1) into matcher trees consumed by the Muxer.AddRoute, L92 call chain.
  • Services. BuildHTTP, L96 resolves a service name into a handler, typically a load balancer built by getLoadBalancerServiceHandler, L435 which proxies to your backends via ProxyBuilder.Build, L41.
  • The API. createRouter, L94 mounts /api/rawdata, /api/overview and the router/service endpoints that power the dashboard at :8080.

The detailed view: static and dynamic configuration types, the merge and model-apply step, per-provider wiring, the HTTP and TCP routing internals, and the observability layer that feeds access logs and metrics.

The Bootstrap Spine: From Binary to First Route

Traefik has one moving picture worth internalizing: configuration flows one way, requests flow the other. Configuration enters at the bottom through providers, gets merged in the middle, and radiates outward to listeners; requests enter at the top through entrypoints and fall down through matchers to services.

In the bootstrap, setupServer, L180 does eight things in order: build the provider aggregator, create the TLS manager, register metric clients and the access log, construct TCP and UDP entrypoints, build the service manager factory, build the router factory, create the configuration watcher, and finally hand everything to NewServer, L403. The Server, L17 type is tiny on purpose — its Start, L47 method just starts the entrypoints and the watcher and then waits on a signal channel. All the intelligence lives in the two halves it connects.

The watcher is the part that makes Traefik feel alive. receiveConfigurations, L98 keeps a map of the latest config per provider, deep-copies and transforms it, and pushes it downstream only when something actually changed; applyConfigurations, L166 then merges everything with mergeConfiguration, L18 and applies the routing model in applyModel, L323. Registered listeners fire after that: TLS configs go to the Manager.UpdateConfigs, L93 method, metrics counters tick, and the switch listener rebuilds routers and swaps them into the live entrypoints via SwitchRouter, L383. A new route exists on the wire without a single connection being dropped.

How Providers Keep the Table Fresh

Every provider implements the same small interface — Provide(channel, pool) — which is why they compose cleanly. The aggregator’s launchProvider, L205 runs each one with optional throttling, so a chatty provider cannot starve the rest.

The file provider is the simplest mental model: Provide, L55 decodes YAML or TOML into a dynamic configuration and, when watching is enabled, addWatcher, L169 attaches fsnotify watchers so an edit is a reload. The Docker provider does the same trick over the Docker API: Provide, L53 lists containers and turns labels into routers and services. The Kubernetes provider is the heavyweight: Provide, L98 watches IngressRoutes and related CRDs, and loadConfigurationFromCRD, L248 converts those objects into Traefik’s own config vocabulary. If you are coming from a Kubernetes background, our Kubernetes primer covers how pods, services and ingress controllers fit together; Traefik simply participates in that world as the controller that consumes the custom resources.

One provider deserves a special mention even though it ships no services: the internal one, named "internal" at ProviderName, L22. It contributes the api@internal and dashboard services that the API handler serves, and it is the provider the watcher waits for before applying the first configuration.

How a Request Flows Through the Routing Core

A request hits an entrypoint socket, is accepted by the loop in Start, L255, and is handed to the current TCP router through a handler switcher. The TCP router at ServeTCP, L101 peeks at the first bytes to decide TLS or plain TCP, routes on SNI where applicable, and for HTTP traffic forwards the connection into a Go HTTP server where the real matching begins.

That matching is the muxer: ServeHTTP, L48 walks registered routes and dispatches to the first matcher tree that returns true. Router priority, provider precedence and negated matchers all resolve here. Before the match even happens, the request has already passed through the entrypoint chain built by newHTTPServer, L643 — forwarded-header handling, path normalization and keep-alive limits.

Once a router matches, the middleware chain built by BuildMiddlewareChain, L69 wraps the service handler: rate limiting, circuit breaking, retries, header manipulation, or your own chain of middlewares. Observability wraps everything: the observability manager defined at ObservabilityMgr, L23 wires metrics and tracing, and the access log handler’s ServeHTTP, L190 captures request and response fields for every round trip, logged after the response completes in logTheRoundTrip, L355. For inference traffic, that access log line — with the router name, service name and duration — is often the cheapest per-request telemetry you can get, and it exports cleanly to a Prometheus setup alongside Traefik’s own metrics endpoints, ready for dashboards once you wire in Grafana.

Finally the service layer. BuildHTTP, L96 rejects multi-type services, checks for recursion, and builds the handler: weighted round robin at getWRRServiceHandler, L323, mirroring at getMirrorServiceHandler, L286, failover, or a plain proxy. The resulting proxy, built through NewProxyBuilder, L29, is where your request finally leaves Traefik for a backend — with connection pooling, transport settings and TLS handled by the transport manager configured from serversTransports.

From Install to Your First Model

The fastest path is a single container run straight from the README:

docker run -d -p 8080:8080 -p 80:80 -v $PWD/traefik.toml:/etc/traefik/traefik.toml traefik

That maps the dashboard port 8080 and the HTTP port 80, and mounts one TOML file. The minimal static side of that file matches the repository’s own sample:

[entryPoints]
  [entryPoints.web]
    address = ":80"

[api]
  dashboard = true

Static configuration — entrypoints, providers, the API — is read once at startup and describes what Traefik listens on. Everything dynamic lives with the providers. The two-level split is enforced in the type system: static.Configuration at Configuration, L86 with its EntryPoints map at L90, versus dynamic.Configuration at Configuration, L23 holding routers, services, middlewares and TLS.

Now point it at something real. Suppose your inference backend is a FastAPI service exposing /v1/embeddings; our FastAPI walkthrough shows how to build one. Add a dynamic file next to the static one:

[http]
  [http.routers.to-model-api]
    rule = "Host(`api.example.com`) && PathPrefix(`/v1`)"
    service = "model-api"

  [http.services.model-api.loadBalancer]
    [[http.services.model-api.loadBalancer.servers]]
      url = "http://10.0.0.11:8000"
    [[http.services.model-api.loadBalancer.servers]]
      url = "http://10.0.0.12:8000"

Save it, and the file provider’s fsnotify watcher fires, the watcher merges and broadcasts, the router factory rebuilds, and SwitchRouter puts the new route live — no restart, no dropped connections. Two servers in the load balancer means you already have failover; to canary a new model version, add a third server with a low weight, watch the access logs and metrics, then shift the weight as confidence grows. On Kubernetes, the same result comes from an IngressRoute CRD instead of a TOML block, watched continuously by the CRD provider — and remember that token streaming backends need generous read timeouts so long generations are not cut mid-stream.

Honest Limits

  • Configuration plumbing is YAML/TOML/labels, not code. Routing rules are expressive but stringly typed; complex header surgery or request rewriting logic belongs in your application or a dedicated middleware, not in ever-longer rule expressions.
  • No built-in token-aware routing. Traefik balances requests, not tokens or model latency. If you want routing decisions based on prompt size or per-token cost, you build that in the application tier behind the proxy.
  • Watch the timeout defaults for LLM traffic. Long streaming responses are fine over HTTP, but aggressive responding timeouts on an entrypoint will truncate slow generations; set read and write timeouts deliberately for inference entrypoints.
  • The dashboard is a window, not a control plane. It exposes runtime state read-only (plus ACME user actions); fleet changes still flow through your providers — GitOps, Kubernetes CRDs or files.
  • Deep Kubernetes integration means CRDs. Native Kubernetes Ingress support is limited compared to the CRD provider; to use Traefik fully in a cluster you adopt its custom resource definitions, which is a real ecosystem commitment.

Where does Traefik sit in the stack? Above the service mesh and below your application frameworks: it terminates TLS at the edge, keeps a live map of your fleet, and routes with enough middleware depth to protect expensive GPU-backed services from accidental overload. Read the bootstrap once with the diagrams open and the whole design — providers feeding a watcher feeding swappable routers — is one of the cleaner pieces of Go infrastructure code you will find.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of Traefik: entrypoints, rule parsing, hot-reload watchers, providers, load balancers and the API behind the dashboard.

entry.title: etcd: The Tiny Consensus Machine Holding Kubernetes Together

link.title: etcd: The Tiny Consensus Machine Holding Kubernetes Together

entry.content:
If you train or serve machine-learning systems on Kubernetes, every meaningful thing you do passes through a small Go program you have probably never looked at. When the scheduler decides which node runs your GPU job, it reads and writes keys in etcd. When a Deployment rolls out a new model server, the desired state lives in etcd. When an operator leader election picks which replica reconciles your custom resource, the lease that decides the winner is an etcd lease. Kubernetes stores the entire cluster state — every Pod, Secret, ConfigMap, and CRD — as keys in etcd, which is why etcd outages take down clusters and why etcd backups are the first thing every serious operator configures.

etcd itself is a CNCF-graduated, distributed key-value store written in Go. Its contract is unusually strict for a database: writes must survive the loss of minority members and never disagree between replicas, even under partitions. To deliver that, etcd replicates every mutation through the Raft consensus algorithm before acknowledging it, persists the Raft log in a write-ahead log, and keeps the actual key-value data in an MVCC (multi-version concurrency control) store where every transaction creates a new global revision. On top of that sits a gRPC API with three killer features: atomic transactions (Txn), range queries with history, and low-latency Watch streams that push changes instead of forcing clients to poll. The project’s own README describes it as simple, secure, fast (benchmarked 10,000 writes/sec), and reliable — a fair summary of what the code actually implements.

For AI infrastructure specifically, etcd is the coordination primitive hiding under everything else. Job queues built on leases, model registries that need strongly consistent metadata, service discovery for inference replicas, distributed locks for training coordination — all of these are tiny protocols layered on etcd’s primitives. Reading its source is one of the best ways to understand how a “boring” piece of infrastructure earns the right to be boring. In this tour we walk the etcd-io/etcd repository (branch main), from the client stubs to the disk, with every symbol below verified against the real code.

The write path at a glance: a gRPC client proposal flows through the Raft loop and the write-ahead log, comes back as a committed entry, and is applied to the MVCC store, which then notifies watchers.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts with a client. clientv3.New, L86 dials your endpoints and hands out typed interfaces; the KV interface, L38 defines Put, Get, and Txn in a single screen of code.
  • The wire format is defined once in protobuf. The service KV, L33 declares Range, Put, Txn, Watch, and the lease RPCs that both the client and server compile against.
  • On the server, EtcdServer.Put, L296 receives the request and routes it into raftRequest, L1014, the funnel through which every mutation must pass.
  • raftNode.start, L174 is the beating heart: a loop that ticks the consensus state machine, collects Ready batches, and persists them via WAL.Save, L1000 before the leader ships messages through Transport.Send, L176.
  • Once a majority has persisted an entry, it comes back committed and Apply, L27 decodes it into an internal request for the applier stack.
  • The applier finally touches the store: storeTxnWrite.put, L223 stamps the key with a new revision, writes it into the bolt-backed bucket, and updates the in-memory index.
  • Reads are different: EtcdServer.Range, L107 never goes through Raft for the data itself; serializable reads hit the local store directly, while linearizable reads use a ReadIndex round to prove the serving node’s leadership is still current.
  • Every applied change also wakes the watch machinery: notify, L470 pushes events to watchers that are keeping up, and syncWatchers, L347 replays history for those that fell behind.

The full detail map: eight subsystems from the clientv3 package down to bolt buckets, leases, and the compaction sweep that keeps history bounded.

Two Roads Through the Server

etcd’s elegance comes from treating reads and writes completely differently. A write is a proposal: the server wraps your PutRequest inside an InternalRaftRequest, L22 envelope and calls processInternalRaftRequestOnce, L1060, which blocks until the proposal is either committed and applied, or times out. There is deliberately no fast path — even a single-node cluster takes the full Raft round trip, because the log is the database. The entry, once committed, is handed to applyEntries, L1180, which feeds each one into the applier.

The applier is a layered decorator chain rather than a switch statement. uberApplier.Apply, L82 runs the request through corrupt-store and capped-quota wrappers, then auth and quota checks, before applierV3backend.Put, L50 finally executes the mutation. The dispatch logic itself lives at dispatch, L93, where the wrapper’s non-nil field selects the operation. txn.Put, L30 handles the quirky options (ignore_value, ignore_lease, prev_kv return), and txn.Txn, L32 evaluates the if/then/else comparison trees that make etcd usable as a distributed lock service. Reads skip all of this: txn.Range, L47 executes against a read view of the store, and only the ReadIndex round in requestCurrentIndex, L148 touches consensus — a design that lets reads scale without weakening the consistency contract.

MVCC: Every Write Is a New Revision

The storage layer is where etcd earns its reliability reputation. The core is the store, L53 in server/storage/mvcc, which pairs a bolt database on disk with an in-memory treeIndex. Writing starts at store.Write, L174, which opens a transaction and returns a TxnWrite view. Inside storeTxnWrite.put, L223 you can read the whole scheme in twenty lines: the current revision is packed into orderable bytes by RevToBytes, L54, the marshalled KeyValue is written into the schema.Key, L43 bucket with the revision as its key, and the treeIndex, L39 gets a pointer so that treeIndex.Get, L68 can later resolve any key at any past revision.

This is why etcd can answer “what did this key look like last Tuesday” and why watches can replay history. It is also why history must be pruned: nothing deletes old revisions automatically. scheduleCompaction, L28 periodically discards revisions older than the compaction point, both in bolt and in the index — which is why unwatched, un-compacted etcd clusters grow forever, and why compaction plus defragmentation appear on every etcd operations checklist. Leases tie into the same transaction: storeTxnWrite.put, L223 attaches or detaches keys from leases at le.Attach, L285, and the lessor, L145 in server/lease handles Grant, L281 and Renew, L396 — the primitive behind Kubernetes leader elections and TTL-based liveness checks.

Watches Without Polling

The Watch RPC declared at rpc.proto, L98 is the feature that made etcd the substrate for controllers. On the client side, NewWatcher, L252 opens a single gRPC stream that can multiplex thousands of individual watches, each created with watcher.Watch, L304. On the server side, a write transaction in the watchable store collects its changes and, at commit, watchableStoreTxnWrite.End, L22 calls into notify, L470, which batches events per watcher and sends them on the watcher’s channel. A watcher whose channel is full is demoted to a “victim” rather than dropped — the event history in MVCC is the safety net, and syncWatchers, L347 later replays the missed range from the store.

The consequence for system builders is profound: you never poll. A controller reacts to state changes in milliseconds, and because events carry the revision, a resuming client can ask for exactly what it missed. Kubernetes controllers, service-discovery clients, and configuration reloaders are all just watch loops over this mechanism. Compared with a traditional message broker’s fire-and-forget delivery, an etcd watch is a strongly consistent event stream over a compacted log, with the twist that the log is also the authoritative database.

From Install to Your First Put

The quickest path is the pre-built release binaries from the project’s releases page, available for Linux, macOS, Windows, and Docker. Unpack, then run the single-binary cluster:

./etcd

That is the entire cluster setup for local development: etcd comes up listening on port 2379 for client traffic and 2380 for peer-to-peer replication. In another terminal, use the bundled control tool:

etcdctl put mykey "this is awesome"
etcdctl get mykey

You have just exercised the full path from this tour: the Put was proposed through Raft, persisted in the WAL, applied to the MVCC store, and the Get served from a read view of that store. From Go code, go get go.etcd.io/etcd/client/v3 gives you the same operations through clientv3. For production-grade durability you would run three or five members on separate machines — the quorum math is what turns three modest servers into a store that tolerates one failure with zero data loss. If you run Kubernetes, you already operate such a cluster; the storage engines we toured in the message-broker pieces — NATS and Kafka — solve different problems and complement etcd rather than replace it, and Prometheus is the standard way to watch an etcd cluster’s health metrics.

Honest Limits

etcd is not a general-purpose database, and the source makes the limits explicit. Its README’s 10,000 writes/sec benchmark headline comes with a real cost: every write is fsynced into the WAL and committed by consensus, so etcd will never compete with Redis or Kafka on raw throughput — it is designed for small, critical metadata (Kubernetes recommends keeping values under 1 MB and the store below a few GB). History is only as deep as your compaction policy; disable compaction and the store grows without bound, enable it too aggressively and slow watchers lose the events they need. Raft gives you linearizable writes, but a watch stream is eventually delivered — a client that disconnects relies on replay, not a guarantee of at-least-once push. And leases are TTL-based best-effort liveness: a GC pause longer than your TTL can falsely expire a lock holder, a failure mode every lease-based leader election must handle. None of this is a flaw — it is the honest price of the strongest consistency guarantees in the industry, and reading the code shows exactly where each guarantee is enforced.

entry.title: InfluxDB 3: A Source Tour of the Rust, Arrow, and Parquet Time-Series Engine

link.title: InfluxDB 3: A Source Tour of the Rust, Arrow, and Parquet Time-Series Engine

entry.content:
Anyone who has trained a model or operated a GPU cluster knows the feeling: the metrics are everywhere and the answers are nowhere. GPU utilization counters, temperature probes, token latencies, loss curves from experiment trackers, queue depths from an inference server — all of it arrives as small, append-heavy, time-ordered records, all of it wants to be written right now, and most questions you ask later are about “the most recent value” or “the last hour.” That workload profile is exactly what a time-series database (TSDB) is built for, which is why TSDBs sit underneath ML platforms: they absorb telemetry at line rate and answer dashboards, alerts, and drift checks without a full-scan tax. If you have read our tours of VictoriaMetrics, TimescaleDB, or ClickHouse, you know how differently each system answers that question.

InfluxDB 3 Core is InfluxData’s answer, rebuilt from the ground up. The project describes itself as “powered by Apache Arrow, DataFusion, and Parquet”: writes arrive as InfluxDB line protocol, rows are held as Arrow RecordBatches in memory, queries run through the DataFusion engine, and the durable format is Parquet files on object storage — S3, Azure, GCP buckets, or just the local disk with no dependencies. The project has been generally available since April 2025, and its feature list reads like a wishlist for observability on a budget: a diskless architecture with object storage support, sub-10 ms last-value queries from an in-memory cache, an embedded Python VM for plugins and triggers, and compatibility with the 1.x/2.x write APIs and the InfluxQL query language.

One clarification before we dive in: the default branch of influxdata/influxdb on GitHub is main, and that branch hosts the InfluxDB 3 Core codebase — a Rust workspace of about thirty crates. The older, pre-Rewrite generations of InfluxDB live on separate branches of the same repository: the 2.x code (Go and Flux, with its TSM storage engine) is on main-2.x, and the venerable 1.x code is on master-1.x. Nothing in this tour touches those branches; every file and line number below comes from the Rust code on main, verified directly against the working tree; the two diagrams below were generated from that same tree.

Overview of InfluxDB 3 Core on the main branch: the influxdb3 binary wires an HTTP API, a write buffer, Parquet persistence, and a DataFusion-backed query executor into one server.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • fn main, L4 is the entry point of the influxdb3 server binary, which fans out into clap-based subcommands.
  • command, L952 is the serve command: it resolves configuration, constructs the object store, and assembles the runtime.
  • HttpApi, L1040 holds the two halves of the system — a write_buffer and a query_executor — behind one HTTP interface.
  • API_V3_WRITE, L5 names the /api/v3/write_lp route; sibling constants define /api/v3/query_sql, /api/v2/write, and the legacy /write endpoints.
  • WriteBufferImpl, L170 is the ingest heart: it validates line protocol rows, appends them to the WAL, and hands them to the queryable buffer.
  • QueryableBuffer, L44 keeps recent data as in-memory Arrow chunks and doubles as the WAL’s file notifier.
  • Persister, L128 is, in the code’s own words, “the primary interface with object storage where InfluxDB stores all Parquet.”
  • QueryExecutorImpl, L61 wraps the DataFusion/IOx execution layer so SQL and InfluxQL plans can read both buffered chunks and persisted Parquet.

The detailed view adds the CLI flags, route dispatch, WAL mechanics, per-table buffers, and the Parquet persistence calls that the overview collapses into single boxes.

The Write Path: Line Protocol to WalOp

Everything starts with an HTTP POST. The route_request, L2671 dispatch table matches (Method::POST, API_V3_WRITE) to the write handler, and write_lp, L1107 pulls parameters — db, precision, accept_partial, no_sync — straight from the URL query string. write_lp_inner, L1113 validates the database name, decodes the UTF-8 body, and calls into the buffer with the server’s clock as the default timestamp.

Inside the buffer, write_lp, L464 parses and validates the line protocol, and write_lp_inner, L505 converts valid lines into buffered data. The interesting commitment comes next: valid rows become a WalOp::Write, L541 and are pushed through write_ops_unconfirmed, L544. The comment in the code explains the contract — the WAL buffers ops in memory and, once per flush interval (about a second by default), persists them as a single WAL file in the configured object store. When that happens, the QueryableBuffer, L44 is notified: it was registered as the WAL’s file_notifier at construction time (L429), and its buffer_write_ops, L575 applies the batch into per-table buffers. The TableBuffer, L46 chunks by time (buffer_chunk, L113) and can turn any chunk into partitioned Arrow RecordBatches on demand — so data is queryable within milliseconds, long before it is durable as Parquet. Replay on restart follows the same edges in reverse: the WAL instance is created only after the persisted snapshot list is loaded, then feeds the buffer back into a queryable state.

From Line Protocol to Parquet: The Storage Side

The WAL is the short-term journal; Parquet is the long-term memory. Snapshots are the hinge between them: persist_snapshot, L370 writes the snapshot’s file list to object storage, which is what allows old WAL files to be dropped. The actual conversion happens in serialize_to_parquet, L202, which runs an Arrow ArrowWriter over the RecordBatches, and persist_parquet_file, L986, which writes those bytes to the object store and returns metadata used to prime the parquet cache. The PersistedFiles, L28 index tracks what has already landed, grouped by month, so the query planner can prune files it does not need.

Two design choices stand out. First, file paths are prefixed by the node identifier — the --node-id flag (L794) exists precisely so multiple servers sharing one bucket do not collide. Second, this OSS workspace persists “Gen1” Parquet files and stops there: there is no compactor crate in the tree you clone from main. Background compaction (merging Gen1 files into larger, query-optimized files) is part of the commercial InfluxDB 3 Enterprise story, and the open-source tree simply does not include it. The Persister, L128 also owns the read side of storage with load_parquet_file, L361 — worth remembering when you wonder who fetches cold data back.

The Query Side: DataFusion Over Everything

On reads, InfluxDB 3 Core is essentially an Arrow-native SQL engine with two data sources stitched together. QueryExecutorImpl, L61 holds the IOx/DataFusion Executor and a per-database Database, L532 registry that exposes each table’s buffered chunks and Parquet files to the planner. Execution bottoms out in execute_stream, L339, where the session context streams RecordBatches out of the physical plan. The HTTP handler query_sql, L1198 accepts GET with db and q URL parameters or POST with a JSON body, and renders results as pretty tables, CSV, JSON, or Parquet. A gRPC side exists too: the FlightSQL service in grpc.rs, L12 lets Arrow-native clients run the same plans over the Flight protocol, and an InfluxQL compatibility layer translates the old 1.x query language. The README’s claim of last-value queries under 10 ms comes from this layer’s distinct-value and last-value caches — QueryableBuffer, L44 collaborates with the distinct and last cache managers that the WriteBuffer trait composes in lib.rs, L66.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps installation honest: Docker images, Debian and RPM packages, and tarballs are on the InfluxData downloads page, and both Core and Enterprise have getting-started guides on docs.influxdata.com. Building from source is documented in CONTRIBUTING.md for contributors. Once installed, the server binary is influxdb3, and the serve command wires everything you saw above. The essential flags, all verified in the CLI definitions: --node-id names the node and prefixes every object store path; --object-store file selects the local filesystem as storage (per the crate’s own docs you must also set --data-dir, which defaults to a .influxdb3 directory); and --http-bind controls the listener, defaulting to 0.0.0.0:8181 per DEFAULT_HTTP_BIND_ADDR, L101. For a throwaway local experiment you can add --without-auth (L319); otherwise the server provisions an admin token through create_admin_token, L1150 on first start. A GET /health endpoint exists for readiness checks.

With the server listening on port 8181, your first write uses the route we traced: POST line protocol to /api/v3/write_lp with a db query parameter. Feeding it a GPU-telemetry-shaped line is the natural demo:

curl -X POST 'http://localhost:8181/api/v3/write_lp?db=demo' \
  -d 'gpu_temp,host=h0,gpu=a100_1 value=71.5'

The response is HTTP 204 when every line was valid — the handler returns the empty body path only when invalid_lines is empty, and otherwise reports the partial write failure. Then query it back with SQL over /api/v3/query_sql, where db selects the database and q carries the SQL text (both names are serde renames on the request struct, so they apply to GET and POST alike):

curl 'http://localhost:8181/api/v3/query_sql?db=demo&q=SELECT+*+FROM+gpu_temp'

What makes this loop satisfying for ML telemetry specifically: the measurement you just created behaves like a table immediately, and the same SQL runs against the hot buffer and the cold Parquet without you choosing. Point your training script’s metrics at /api/v3/write_lp, point Grafana or a notebook at /api/v3/query_sql, and you have a complete “your first model” story: a durable, queryable record of how every experiment behaved.

How the Catalog Holds It Together

One more crate deserves a paragraph: the catalog. Every write and every query touches metadata — which databases exist, which tables belong to them, column types, retention policies. The write buffer exposes it via catalog, L793, returning an Arc<Catalog> from the influxdb3_catalog crate, and the HTTP layer leans on it for token management too. This is a deliberate architectural split in the 3.x design: the catalog is serialized metadata that survives independently of the data files, and the write path consults it to validate incoming lines before any WAL op exists. The trait layering in the write crate — WriteBuffer composing Bufferer, ChunkContainer, DistinctCacheManager, and LastCacheManager from lib.rs, L66 — keeps that metadata-adjacent logic swappable and testable. For the server assembly itself, Server, L151 is built from a CreateServerArgs bundle and serve, L366 drives the accept loop — the final edge in our detail diagram.

Honest Limits

No source tour is complete without the fine print, and InfluxDB 3 Core has a clear one: what you clone from main is the open-source single-node core, and the clustering, replication, and compaction machinery that large deployments want live in the separate, closed-source Enterprise product — the README is explicit that the commercial code is kept separate, and links distinct getting-started guides for Core and Enterprise. Concretely, the OSS tree persists Gen1 Parquet files and relies on the WAL and caches for speed; you will not find a compactor crate here. Second, version archaeology in this repository is unusual: main is InfluxDB 3 Core in Rust, main-2.x is the 2.x generation (the Go/Flux era), and master-1.x is the original 1.x engine — same repository, three different databases. If you are migrating an old 1.x/2.x deployment, the compatibility write APIs and InfluxQL ease that jump, but the storage engines share nothing. Finally, the numbers in this post are code-verified structure, not benchmarks: the README’s sub-10 ms last-value claim is the vendor’s, and your cardinality, disk, and hardware will decide your truth. For adjacent reading, our DuckDB tour pairs well here if you want a second Arrow-native engine to compare against.
